SOURCE ESSAY:
I have been reading a little book called How to Write for the Press. Other books which have been published upon the same subject are How to Be an Author, How to Write a Play, How to Succeed as a Journalist, How to Write for the Magazines, and How to Earn £600 a Year with the Pen. Of these the last-named has, I think, the most pleasing title. Anybody can write a play; the trouble is to get it produced. Almost anybody can be an author; the business is to collect money and fame from this state of being. Writing for the magazines, again, sounds a delightful occupation, but literally it means nothing without the co- operation of the editors of the magazines, and it is this co- operation which is so difficult to secure. But to earn £600 a year with the pen is to do a definite thing; if the book could really tell the secret of that, it would have an enormous sale. I have not read it, so I cannot say what the secret is. Perhaps it was only a handbook on forgery.

How to Write for the Press disappointed me. It is concerned not with the literary journalist (as I believe he is called) but with the reporter (as he is never called, the proper title being "special representative"). It gives in tabular form a list of the facts you should ascertain at the different functions you attend; with this book in your pocket there would be no excuse if you neglected to find out at a wedding the names of the bride and bridegroom. It also gives—and I think this is very friendly of it—a list of useful synonyms for the principal subjects, animate and inanimate, of description. The danger of calling the protagonists at the court of Hymen (this one is not from the book; I thought of it myself just now)—the danger of calling them "the happy pair" more than once in a column is that your readers begin to suspect that you are a person of extremely limited mind, and when once they get this idea into their heads they are not in a proper state to appreciate the rest of your article. But if in your second paragraph you speak of "the joyful couple," and in your third of "the ecstatic brace," you give an impression of careless mystery of the language which can never be shed away.

Among the many interesting chapters is one dealing with contested elections. One of the questions to which the special representative was advised to find an answer was this: "What outside bodies are taking active part in the contest?" In the bad old days—now happily gone for ever—the outside bodies of dead cats used to take an active and important part in the contest, and as the same body would often be used twice the reporter in search of statistics was placed in a position of great responsibility. Nowadays, I suppose, he is only meant to concern himself with such bodies as the Coal Consumers' League and the Tariff Reform League, and there would be no doubt in the mind of anybody as to whether they were there or not.

I am afraid I should not be a success as "our special representative." I should never think of half the things which occur to the good reporter. You read in your local paper a sentence like this: "The bride's brother, who only arrived last week from Australia, where he held an important post under the Government, and is about to proceed on a tour through Canada with—curiously enough—a nephew of the bride-groom, gave her away." Well, what a mass of information has to be gleaned before that sentence can be written. Or this. "The hall was packed to suffocation, and beneath the glare of the electric light— specially installed for this occasion by Messrs. Ampère & Son of Pumpton, the building being at ordinary times strikingly deficient in the matter of artificial lighting in spite of the efforts of the more progressive members of the town council—the faces of not a few of the fairer sex could be observed." You know, I am afraid I should have forgotten all that. I should simply have obtained a copy of the principal speech, and prefaced it with the words," Mr. Dodberry then spoke as follows"; or, if my conscience would not allow of such a palpable misstatement, "Mr. Dodberry then rose with the intention of speaking as follows."

In the more human art of interviewing I should be equally at fault. The interview itself would be satisfactory, but I am afraid that its publication would lead people to believe that all the best things had been said by me. To remember what anybody else has said is easy; to remember, even five minutes after, what one has said oneself is almost impossible. For to recall YOUR remarks in our argument at the club last night is simply a matter of memory; to recall MINE, I have to forget all that I meant to have said, all that I ought to have said, and all that I have thought upon the subject since.

In fact, I begin to see that the successful reporter must eliminate his personality altogether, whereas the successful literary journalist depends for his success entirely upon his personality —which is what is meant by "style." I suppose it is for this reason that, when the literary journalist is sent as "our extra-special representative" to report a prize fight or a final cup tie or a political meeting, the result is always appalling. The "ego" bulges out of every line, obviously conscious that it is showing us no ordinary reporting, determined that it will not be overshadowed by the importance of the subject. And those who are more interested in the matter than in the manner regard him as an intruder, and the others regret that he is so greatly overtaxing his strength.

So each to his business, and his handbook to each—How to Write for the Press to the special representative, and How to Be an Author to the author. There is no book, I believe, called How to Be a Solicitor, or a doctor or an admiral or a brewer. That is a different matter altogether; but any fool can write for the papers.

message.content:
I recently came across a small book titled How to Write for the Press. Other publications on similar topics include How to Be an Author, How to Write a Play, How to Succeed as a Journalist, How to Write for the Magazines, and How to Earn £600 a Year with the Pen. Of these, I find the latter to possess the most appealing title. It seems anyone can write a play; the real challenge lies in getting it staged. Similarly, one can become an author, but the true task is to garner both financial reward and recognition from this pursuit. Writing for magazines may sound like a delightful endeavor, yet it requires the cooperation of editors—a collaboration that is often elusive. Conversely, earning a steady £600 annually through writing presents a tangible goal; if this book could genuinely reveal the secret to achieving that, it would likely be a bestseller. However, as I haven't read it, I can't comment on its contents—perhaps it merely serves as a guide to forgery.

My experience with How to Write for the Press was somewhat disappointing. The focus is not on the literary journalist, as I had anticipated, but rather on the reporter, who is often referred to as a "special representative." The book provides a handy checklist of facts to gather at various events you might attend. Armed with this guide, there would be little excuse for failing to learn the names of the bride and groom at a wedding. Additionally, it offers a list of synonyms for common subjects of description, which I find to be quite generous. The risk of repeatedly labeling the wedding couple as "the happy pair" is that readers may begin to question the writer's intellect. Once that notion takes root, it can cloud their ability to appreciate the rest of the article. However, by diversifying the language—referring to them as "the joyful couple" in one paragraph and "the ecstatic brace" in another—a sense of linguistic intrigue is established that captivates the reader.

Among its many intriguing sections, the book features a chapter dedicated to contested elections. One piece of advice provided to the special representative is to identify which external organizations are actively involved in the contest. In the past, when times were less savory, one might have pointed to the presence of dead cats as a significant outside influence. Thankfully, those days are long gone, and today, one is more likely to encounter organizations such as the Coal Consumers' League or the Tariff Reform League, leaving no ambiguity about their participation.

I must admit, I doubt I would excel in the role of "our special representative." The insights that a proficient reporter gathers would likely escape me. When reading a local paper, you might encounter a sentence like this: "The bride's brother, who only arrived last week from Australia, where he held an important position under the Government, and is about to embark on a tour through Canada with—curiously enough—a nephew of the bridegroom, gave her away." What a wealth of information is required to craft that sentence! Or consider this: "The hall was packed to suffocation, and beneath the glare of the electric light—specially installed for this occasion by Messrs. Ampère & Son of Pumpton, the building typically being strikingly deficient in artificial lighting despite the efforts of the more progressive members of the town council—the faces of not a few of the fairer sex could be observed." In truth, I would likely overlook such details. My approach might be to simply obtain a copy of the main speech and precede it with the phrase, "Mr. Dodberry then spoke as follows"; or, if I couldn't bring myself to be so blatant, I might say, "Mr. Dodberry then rose with the intention of speaking as follows."

In the more personal and nuanced craft of interviewing, I would find myself equally lacking. While the interview itself might be engaging, I fear that the published piece would give the impression that all the most insightful comments originated from me. Remembering what others have said is relatively straightforward; however, recalling my own remarks shortly after an argument at the club can be quite a challenge. To remember YOUR statements requires merely a memory exercise, but to recollect MINE necessitates forgetting everything I intended to express, everything I felt I should have articulated, and all the reflections I have had since the discussion.

I am beginning to understand that a successful reporter must suppress their personality, while a literary journalist's success hinges on their individual voice—what is often referred to as "style." This distinction explains why, when a literary journalist is assigned to cover a prize fight, a cup final, or a political rally as "our extra-special representative," the outcome tends to be lackluster. The writer's ego often overwhelms the narrative, as it strives to ensure that its unique voice is not overshadowed by the significance of the event. Those who are truly invested in the subject matter perceive the journalist as an unwelcome presence, while others lament that the writer is overextending themselves.

Thus, everyone has their own domain, and each has its corresponding handbook—How to Write for the Press serves the special representative, while How to Be an Author caters to the writer. I do not believe there exists a book titled How to Be a Solicitor, or a doctor, an admiral, or a brewer. Those pursuits are in a league of their own. However, writing for the newspapers appears to be an endeavor within reach of almost anyone.
